title: ON Classical Education Fall Edition, 2026
author: ON Classical Education
summary: The editors of ON Classical Education, published by the Great Hearts Institute, mark the journal's first anniversary with an editorial overview of the fourteen pieces in its Fall 2026 issue. The headline development is the Empeiria File, a new section by Albert Cheng and Helen Baxendale that uses C.S. Lewis's 'looking at' versus 'looking along' distinction to justify empirical research on classical education's claims. The Pedagogy and Curriculum section covers the physical conditions of Socratic seminars, Latin as a 'dead' language ordered toward authentic texts, civic curriculum on communism and economics, recovering the quadrivium as a path to wonder, and Daniel Buck's use of Isaiah Berlin to argue that constraint can enlarge freedom. Leadership essays address a formative conversation between a new teacher and her headmaster and how classical educators should order lesson objectives. Great Books pieces range from geography in the Iliad and the syllabus as cosmos to constitutional reasoning and Lincoln's Lyceum Address, and two reviews treat children's literature and New Criticism's influence on classical close reading. The editorial frames the issue's mix of questioning and defending practices as the point: an inheritance is something studied, tested, and handed on rather than preserved behind glass.
points: The new Empeiria File will publish accessible research on classical practices such as handwriting, Socratic dialogue, whole-book reading, and knowledge-rich curriculum.
Andrew Ellison's seminar piece argues that stalled discussions often stem from physical conditions like table shape, posture, and audibility rather than weak questions.
Daniel Murphy challenges classical schools that reform humanities teaching while leaving mathematics on a conventional, utilitarian track, proposing a recovered quadrivium.
Daniel Buck applies Berlin's negative and positive liberty to classroom rules, arguing temporary constraints can build future freedom while warning against coercion.
Mark Bauerlein's essay contends that a coherent syllabus presents students with a picture of reality and a meaningful inheritance against media fragmentation.
quotes: Across its first year, ON Classical Education has brought together teachers, school leaders, scholars, writers, scholars, and practitioners to examine the questions and ideas that animate classical education from the deeply practical to the philosophical.

Drawing on C.S. Lewis’s distinction between “looking at” and “looking along” something, Cheng and Baxendale argue that empirical inquiry need not replace the lived experience, philosophical commitments, or practical wisdom of classical educators. It can offer another vantage point.

The culprit may be far more ordinary: the shape of the tables, clutter, posture, closed books, poorly timed breaks, repetitive routines, or students who simply cannot hear one another. Ellison’s larger argument is deceptively simple: the intellectual life of a seminar depends, in part, on its physical conditions.

Classical schools may teach literature, history, and language very differently from conventional schools, he observes, while often retaining nearly the same mathematics sequence and assumptions about what mathematics is for.

Drawing on Isaiah Berlin’s distinction between negative and positive liberty, Buck argues that temporary constraints can enlarge a student’s future freedom, just as scales eventually allow a pianist to play freely. But he also cautions educators to recognize the line between formation and coercion.

A course does more than assemble readings, he argues. It quietly presents students with a picture of reality: what matters, what belongs to the past, what deserves admiration, and whether human achievement forms part of a meaningful inheritance.
Classical education is rooted in an inheritance, but an inheritance is not something we merely preserve behind glass. It is something we study, question, practice, test, teach, and hand on.
